content:
MEETING HEADER
Date: 2026-04-14 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood Solutions Eng); Jordan Lee (CTO, ArboryTech), Priya Nair (Lead ML Eng), Evan Cho (SRE), Lina Park (PM)

Summary:
- Kickoff scoping for a 6-week POC to validate latency, cost, and tail behavior for ArboryTech's conversational assistant workload.
- Focus areas: QPS shape, concurrency, token distribution (input vs output), tail latency percentiles, and test harness for workload replay.
- Agree to exchange anonymized traffic logs and run an initial replay + synthetic burst test.

Topics Covered:
- Current infra & constraints (VPC limits, egress, existing inference stack)
- Traffic shape: diurnal variability, episodic bursts, and skewed token lengths
- Benchmarks: p50/p95/p99 response latency, per-token cost, throughput saturation points
- Success criteria for POC: latency SLOs, CPU/GPU footprint, correctness/regressions, cost baseline
- Next steps and responsibilities

Action items (from meeting):
- See metadata.action_items for owner/due dates (short summary repeated): Alex to share harness; Priya to provide logs; Maya to propose sizing options; Evan to share infra constraints.

TRANSCRIPT:
[00:00] Alex Kim (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're aiming to scope the POC today — specifically how your traffic looks, what success looks like, and how we should benchmark. Jordan, do you want to kick off with a very short overview of the use case?

[00:16] Jordan Lee (ArboryTech): Yeah sure, uh hi all. So ArboryTech runs a customer support assistant embedded in our web and mobile apps. It's mixed use — short intent classification prompts, and longer multi-turn help sessions. Our typical peak is, um, around 1.5k QPS today for the short calls, but there are bursts during campaigns that go to, like, 8k QPS for a few minutes. We're trying to validate whether Redwood Dedicated or hosted will handle this with our p95 SLA and also to estimate cost.

[00:40] Maya Patel (Redwood SE): Great, thanks. Quick clarifying question — is the 1.5k QPS measured as full generation responses, or is that requests that sometimes touch a cached response?

[00:50] Jordan Lee (ArboryTech): It's requests at the API edge; roughly 60% are short single-turn intents with average response tokens ~20, and 40% are multi-turn where output tokens average 180 with input context usually 400 tokens because we include history. So there's a wide distribution.

[01:12] Priya Nair (ArboryTech): Also, note our outputs are trimmed for safe content but we do keep KV-like session state — not KV cache in the infra sense but session state that can be sent as prefix.

[01:22] Maya Patel (Redwood SE): Right, that helps. So we need to model both the high-QPS short path and the long-tail multi-turn sessions. For benchmarking we'll want to reproduce the token distribution and concurrency mix, not just peak RPS.

[01:35] Evan Cho (ArboryTech): Quick question on SLO — we currently target p95 <= 350ms for short responses (<=40 tokens) and p95 <= 1.2s for longer sessions up to 512 tokens. Is that realistic?

[01:50] Diego Ramos (Redwood SE): It's a reasonable starting SLO for hosted inference with optimized batching and KV/prefix caching. For Dedicated with GPUs and optimal quantization we can usually hit <250ms p95 on short 20-token responses, assuming continuous batching and no cold-starts. But long responses will be dominated by generation throughput — p95 around 1s for 512 tokens is tighter but possible with larger batch/window tuning.

[02:15] Jordan Lee (ArboryTech): Can you explain the batching effect? In our system we open many short concurrent sockets, and we worry batching will add latency.

[02:25] Maya Patel (Redwood SE): Absolutely. We do continuous batching — the runtime tries to form batches within a micro-window (tens of ms) to increase GPU utilization while honoring latency SLOs. For ultra-short prompts we might enable async dispatch and smaller batch sizes; for long form we can allow larger batches. The key part of the POC is to test those knobs with your exact concurrency and token mix.

[02:48] Priya Nair (ArboryTech): Another thing — our token distribution is heavy-tailed: 70% of requests output <50 tokens, but 10% are 1k+ tokens (long transcripts). How do you account for those spikes?

[03:03] Maya Patel (Redwood SE): We'll model token skew explicitly in the replay harness. Two approaches: 1) synthetic bursts where we ramp to the observed 99th percentile token lengths and 2) traced replay from your logs to capture real mixtures and temporal correlation. We also have strategies like prefix caching for stable session prefixes to reduce per-request compute.

[03:22] Lina Park (ArboryTech): For privacy we can't share raw transcripts. We'll scrub PII — is that sufficient for benchmarking?

[03:28] Alex Kim (Redwood AE): Yep, scrubbed logs are fine — we only need tokens counts, timings, and anonymized prompt types. The harness accepts an anonymized CSV or ndjson with fields: timestamp, prompt_length_tokens, response_length_tokens, user_session_id (hashed), label (intent).

[03:45] Jordan Lee (ArboryTech): Sounds good. On the dedicated vs hosted question, our security team prefers Dedicated with VPC peering, but we'd like a price/latency comparison.

[03:56] Maya Patel (Redwood SE): For the POC we typically run the same replay against two configs: Hosted (same model family, managed runtime) and Dedicated (reserved GPU pool, pinned model, optional quantization). We measure throughput until saturation and collect p50/p95/p99, GPU utilization, and cost per 1M tokens. That'll give you apples-to-apples.

[04:12] Evan Cho (ArboryTech): Any gotchas with KV cache or session affinity in Dedicated? We have sticky sessions for some flows.

[04:20] Diego Ramos (Redwood SE): Sticky sessions are fine; affinity helps reduce cache misses. Biggest gotchas are bursty reuse patterns where cached prefixes grow; that changes memory footprint on the runtime. We'll instrument KV/attention cache hit rates during the replay so you can see memory vs latency tradeoffs.

[04:36] Priya Nair (ArboryTech): In terms of QPS modeling — we see diurnal variance, mid-day peak, and campaign spikes. Can you replay those shapes or do you need constant-rate runs?

[04:48] Maya Patel (Redwood SE): We can do both. Recommended approach: 1) baseline constant-rate ramps to find saturation curve, 2) replay real diurnal shape from logs, 3) run targeted microbursts at various percentiles (e.g., 98th/99.5th) to test tail behavior and autoscaling. We'll measure autoscaling response, if Dedicated has burst pools configured.

[05:10] Jordan Lee (ArboryTech): About timelines — you suggested 6-week POC earlier. What's a realistic schedule to get to initial benchmark outputs?

[05:18] Alex Kim (Redwood AE): Typical cadence: week 0 (this week) — exchange artifacts and finalize scope; week 1 — Redwood sets up test configs and receives logs; week 2 — initial baseline runs and quick tuning; weeks 3–4 — extended replay and corner-case tests (burst + long tails); week 5 — refine and run validation; week 6 — deliver final report and recommended sizing/pricing. So initial benchmark outputs (baseline numbers and first saturation curves) can be delivered by end of week 2.

[05:44] Priya Nair (ArboryTech): Who will run the replay? Can we run it ourselves in our VPC or do you need to run from Redwood?

[05:52] Maya Patel (Redwood SE): We support both. For security-sensitive customers we provide a harness you can run in your VPC that posts metrics back to the Redwood console or to a prometheus endpoint. For quick comparisons we can run from our infra and provide logs. For ArboryTech I'd recommend running the harness in your VPC for realistic network shapes and to avoid egress limits.

[06:10] Evan Cho (ArboryTech): Good, we'll prefer VPC-run. We'll also need guidance on request shaping so we don't exceed internal egress or API gateway limits during bursts.

[06:18] Diego Ramos (Redwood SE): We'll include a runbook that throttles and shapes according to your limits and still reproduces burst profiles by spacing concurrent clients.

[06:26] Alex Kim (Redwood AE): Quick question for Priya — what percentage of requests are cached or answered by a static KB vs model generation?

[06:34] Priya Nair (ArboryTech): Roughly 25% resolve from internal KB (no full model call), 55% are short generative, and 20% are long generation sessions.

[06:44] Maya Patel (Redwood SE): That KB hit fraction matters because it reduces average token cost but doesn't reduce concurrency pressure at the gateway. We'll parameterize that in the replay harness.

[06:55] Lina Park (ArboryTech): On the success criteria side — besides latency and cost, our product team cares about hallucination rates and correctness regressions. Can Redwood surface regression alerts tied to prompt sets?

[07:06] Alex Kim (Redwood AE): Yes — part of Redwood Optimize is prompt-set based quality monitoring. For the POC we'll run a small holdout suite of ~200 prompts that your team marks as critical; we'll evaluate output consistency and flag token-level divergence and basic correctness metrics. For deeper evals you can hook a human review loop.

[07:28] Jordan Lee (ArboryTech): How do you measure cost? Is it per token or per GPU-hour?

[07:34] Diego Ramos (Redwood SE): For hosted we report per-token plus model-type multipliers (and sometimes a small request overhead). For Dedicated we model cost as reserved GPU capacity plus a measured effective cost per 1M tokens from the benchmark run; we'll show both so you can compare.

[07:48] Priya Nair (ArboryTech): Can you run a short demo of how the harness shows p95/p99 and token distribution?

[07:55] Maya Patel (Redwood SE): Quickly, yes. (screen-shares) Here's a sample run: x-axis time, y-axis request rate; separate panes for response length distribution and per-second concurrency. You can drill into a minute with a burst and see p50/p95/p99 numbers. Note sometimes transcription on our side shows K-V cash instead of KV cache in logs — minor but FYI, we normalize naming.

[08:22] Jordan Lee (ArboryTech): Ha, yeah that mismatch is funny. Alright, on benchmarks — what model family will you suggest? We're currently evaluating a 8B dense vs a 16B quantized.

[08:34] Diego Ramos (Redwood SE): For this mix I'd propose two candidate variants: 1) 8B with int8 quantization for lower latency on short responses, 2) 16B qt (Q4_0 / Q8_0 depending on perf) for higher-quality long-form. We'll run both in the POC to compare cost/quality/latency.

[08:52] Priya Nair (ArboryTech): Any expectation of tokenization differences causing length variance? We currently use a whitespace-ish tokenizer in our offline tooling.

[08:59] Maya Patel (Redwood SE): We'll align tokenizers as part of the harness — token counts must match runtime tokenizer for accurate per-token cost. We'll include a small conversion utility.

[09:10] Jordan Lee (ArboryTech): For the load profiling, we'd like to know the concurrency per session — we have patterns with many simultaneous long sessions, not just many short parallel requests.

[09:19] Diego Ramos (Redwood SE): Absolutely — concurrency profile is critical. We'll instrument two key measures: concurrent in-flight tokens (aggregated) and concurrent sessions. That helps size KV cache memory and GPU context.

[09:33] Evan Cho (ArboryTech): Are there examples of customers with similar burst shapes you can share?

[09:38] Alex Kim (Redwood AE): We can share anonymized case studies — e.g., a telecom customer with 10k microbursts and heavy long-form sessions. We'll attach a short example in the follow-up email.

[09:49] Priya Nair (ArboryTech): On the topic of regressions, will you capture token-level diffs and allow us to re-run failing prompts in a deterministic mode?

[09:58] Maya Patel (Redwood SE): Yes — the harness can run a deterministic seed mode and capture token diffs. We'll flag divergence above thresholds you set.

[10:06] Jordan Lee (ArboryTech): One more operational question — what observability will we get during the POC? Dashboards, logs, tracing?

[10:12] Diego Ramos (Redwood SE): You'll get per-route latency breakdowns, token counts, KV cache hit rates, GPU utilization, and a trace sampler for slow requests. We can stream metrics to your Prometheus or provide temporary console access.

[10:26] Alex Kim (Redwood AE): Great. Let's recap next steps and owners — Alex will send the benchmark harness + runbook; Maya will include the two sizing options and the quantization plan; Priya will provide anonymized logs; Evan will share VPC egress limits; Redwood will prepare an initial Dedicated vs Hosted cost projection.

[10:45] Jordan Lee (ArboryTech): Sounds good. One ask — can you include a small synthetic that stresses 99.9th percentile token lengths? We want to see tail blowups.

[10:54] Maya Patel (Redwood SE): Absolutely — we'll include targeted microburst templates including 99.9th percentile long-session stress.

[11:02] Lina Park (ArboryTech): Also please include a brief security checklist for running the harness in our VPC — keys, least privilege, metrics endpoints, retention.

[11:10] Alex Kim (Redwood AE): Will do. We'll add SAML SSO notes and KMS integration options.

[11:16] Priya Nair (ArboryTech): Good. Thanks everyone — this was productive.

[11:20] Alex Kim (Redwood AE): Thanks — we'll follow up with the artifacts this week and schedule the replay run once we have the logs.

[11:27] (meeting wraps)

NOTES / BENCHMARK PLAN SNIPPET (short):
- Baseline constant-rate ramp: 100 RPS -> 2k RPS -> 5k RPS to find throughput knee.
- Token-aware replay: use anonymized 7-day traffic with token counts to recreate diurnal shape.
- Microburst tests: 30s/60s bursts to 8k QPS at 95th/99th token lengths.
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency (response completion), per-token latency breakdown, GPU util, KV cache hit rate, cost per 1M tokens.
- Quality: run 200 prompt holdout set and compute token-level diffs and simple correctness labels.

END OF TRANSCRIPT
